meta.subject: science
meta.description: Chemistry facts: periodic table, bonding, states of matter, pH, reactions, molar mass, solutions, organic chemistry, electrochemistry

facts.statement: The periodic table organizes elements by increasing atomic number (number of protons)
Elements in the same group (column) have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons
Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells
Metals are typically shiny, good conductors, malleable, and ductile; nonmetals are typically dull, poor conductors, and brittle as solids
The atomic number equals the number of protons, which defines what element it is
Hydrogen (H) is the lightest element with atomic number 1; helium (He) has atomic number 2
Group 18 elements (noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have full outer electron shells and are very unreactive
Group 1 elements (alkali metals: Li, Na, K, etc.) are highly reactive metals with one valence electron
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are isotopes
An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons: cations are positive (lost e-), anions are negative (gained e-)
Group 17 (halogens: F, Cl, Br, I) have 7 valence electrons and are very reactive nonmetals
Atomic mass is the weighted average mass of all isotopes of an element, measured in atomic mass units (amu)
There are 118 confirmed elements on the periodic table as of 2024
The first 20 elements in order: H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, K, Ca
Metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) have properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals; silicon is a semiconductor used in computer chips
Transition metals (groups 3-12) often have multiple oxidation states and form colorful compounds; examples include iron, copper, and gold
Electron configuration describes how electrons are arranged in shells and subshells; the first shell holds up to 2 electrons, the second holds up to 8
Atomic radius generally decreases across a period (left to right) because more protons pull electrons closer, and increases down a group because new shells are added
Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust (about 46% by mass) and the third most abundant element in the universe

common_errors.wrong: the atomic number equals the number of electrons
common_errors.correct: The atomic number equals the number of protons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons, but ions have different electron counts.

common_errors.wrong: all metals are magnetic
common_errors.correct: Only iron, nickel, and cobalt (and their alloys) are strongly magnetic. Most metals are not magnetic.

common_errors.wrong: noble gases never form compounds
common_errors.correct: Noble gases are very unreactive but some (especially xenon) can form compounds under extreme conditions.

common_errors.wrong: isotopes of an element have different chemical properties
common_errors.correct: Isotopes have the same chemical properties (same electrons). They differ in mass and nuclear stability.

common_errors.wrong: the mass number equals the atomic number
common_errors.correct: Atomic number = protons only. Mass number = protons + neutrons. They are different for most elements.

common_errors.wrong: atoms are the smallest things that exist
common_errors.correct: Atoms are made of smaller particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Protons and neutrons are made of even smaller quarks.

common_errors.wrong: electrons orbit the nucleus like planets orbit the Sun
common_errors.correct: Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals) around the nucleus. They do not follow fixed planetary-style paths.

facts.statement: Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating oppositely charged ions that attract each other
Covalent bonds form when atoms share electrons to achieve a stable electron configuration
Metallic bonds involve a sea of shared electrons among metal atoms, giving metals their conductivity and malleability
Ionic compounds typically form between metals and nonmetals; covalent compounds typically form between nonmetals
Valence electrons are the outermost electrons of an atom and determine its chemical bonding behavior
The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to have 8 electrons in their outer shell
A polar covalent bond has unequal sharing of electrons, creating partial charges; water (H2O) has polar bonds
A nonpolar covalent bond has equal sharing of electrons, as in O2 or N2
Lewis dot structures show valence electrons as dots around an element's symbol
Electronegativity measures an atom's ability to attract shared electrons; fluorine is the most electronegative element
Water is a polar molecule, making it an excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances
Hydrogen bonds are weak intermolecular forces between a hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F and a nearby N, O, or F
Van der Waals forces (London dispersion forces) are the weakest intermolecular forces, present in all molecules, caused by temporary fluctuations in electron distribution
Ionic compounds typically have high melting and boiling points because the electrostatic attractions in the crystal lattice are strong
A double bond shares two pairs of electrons between atoms; a triple bond shares three pairs. Multiple bonds are shorter and stronger than single bonds

common_errors.wrong: ionic bonds are stronger than covalent bonds in every case
common_errors.correct: Both bond types can be very strong. Ionic compounds have high melting points due to the lattice structure, not individual bond strength.

common_errors.wrong: covalent bonds involve transferring electrons
common_errors.correct: Covalent bonds involve sharing electrons between atoms. Ionic bonds involve transferring electrons.

common_errors.wrong: all compounds are molecules
common_errors.correct: Ionic compounds (like NaCl) form crystal lattices, not discrete molecules. Only covalently bonded substances form molecules.

common_errors.wrong: hydrogen bonds are as strong as covalent bonds
common_errors.correct: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds. They are intermolecular forces, not chemical bonds.

common_errors.wrong: atoms always follow the octet rule
common_errors.correct: Hydrogen only needs 2 electrons (duet rule). Boron can be stable with 6. Elements in period 3+ can have expanded octets (more than 8 electrons).

facts.statement: The three common states of matter are solid (fixed shape and volume), liquid (fixed volume, takes shape of container), and gas (no fixed shape or volume)
Melting is the change from solid to liquid; freezing is liquid to solid
Evaporation/boiling is the change from liquid to gas; condensation is gas to liquid
Sublimation is the change directly from solid to gas, skipping the liquid phase (e.g., dry ice)
Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees F) and boils at 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees F) at standard pressure
In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions; in liquids, they slide past each other; in gases, they move freely and rapidly
Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance
During a phase change, temperature remains constant even though energy is being added or removed
Plasma is a fourth state of matter consisting of ionized gas, found in stars and lightning
Gases can be compressed because their particles are far apart; solids and liquids are nearly incompressible
Deposition is the phase change from gas directly to solid (the reverse of sublimation); frost forming on windows is an example
The kinetic molecular theory states that all matter is made of constantly moving particles; temperature is a measure of their average kinetic energy
Boyle's Law: at constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional (P1V1 = P2V2)
Charles's Law: at constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V1/T1 = V2/T2)
The ideal gas law combines Boyle's and Charles's laws: PV = nRT, where n is moles and R is the gas constant

common_errors.wrong: ice is colder than water at the freezing point
common_errors.correct: Ice and water can exist at exactly 0 degrees C. During melting, both are at the same temperature.

common_errors.wrong: steam and water vapor are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Water vapor is invisible gas. The white cloud you see is steam (tiny water droplets), which forms when vapor condenses in cooler air.

common_errors.wrong: matter cannot change states
common_errors.correct: All matter can change states with sufficient temperature or pressure changes. Even metals become gases at high enough temperatures.

common_errors.wrong: gases have no mass
common_errors.correct: Gases have mass. Air at sea level has a density of about 1.2 kg/m^3. A room full of air weighs dozens of kilograms.

common_errors.wrong: evaporation and boiling are the same process
common_errors.correct: Evaporation occurs only at the surface at any temperature. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at the boiling point, with bubbles of vapor forming inside.

facts.statement: The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14: acids below 7, neutral at 7, bases above 7
Acids produce hydrogen ions (H+) in solution; bases produce hydroxide ions (OH-) in solution
Pure water has a pH of 7, which is neutral
Each whole number change in pH represents a tenfold change in acidity or basicity
Common acids include hydrochloric acid (HCl, pH ~1), vinegar (acetic acid, pH ~3), and lemon juice (citric acid, pH ~2)
Common bases include bleach (pH ~13), baking soda (pH ~8.5), and ammonia (pH ~11)
An acid-base neutralization reaction produces water and a salt: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O
Litmus paper turns red in acids and blue in bases; phenolphthalein is colorless in acids and pink in bases
A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
Human blood has a pH of about 7.4 (slightly basic) and is buffered to maintain this level
Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) has a pH of about 1.5-3.5, which is needed to digest proteins and kill bacteria
An Arrhenius acid donates H+ ions in solution; a Bronsted-Lowry acid donates protons to another substance
Antacids work by neutralizing excess stomach acid; they typically contain bases like calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide

common_errors.wrong: all acids are dangerous and can burn you
common_errors.correct: Many acids are mild and safe, like citric acid in oranges and acetic acid in vinegar.

common_errors.wrong: a pH of 0 means there is no acid
common_errors.correct: A pH of 0 is extremely acidic (like battery acid). pH 7 is neutral. Lower pH = more acidic, not less.

common_errors.wrong: bases are not dangerous because they are not acids
common_errors.correct: Strong bases (like concentrated lye/NaOH) can cause severe chemical burns, just like strong acids.

common_errors.wrong: pH 3 is only slightly more acidic than pH 6
common_errors.correct: Each pH unit is a 10x change. pH 3 is 1,000 times more acidic than pH 6 (10^3 = 1000).

common_errors.wrong: all acids taste sour and all bases taste bitter
common_errors.correct: While many acids are sour and many bases are bitter, you should NEVER taste chemicals to identify them. Many are toxic.

common_errors.wrong: neutral pH means the solution has no ions
common_errors.correct: At pH 7, water still has equal concentrations of H+ and OH- ions (10^-7 M each). Neutral means the concentrations are balanced, not absent.

facts.statement: In a chemical reaction, reactants are transformed into products; atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed (conservation of mass)
A balanced chemical equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides
Exothermic reactions release heat energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb heat energy
A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed in the reaction
Combustion reactions involve a substance reacting with oxygen, often producing carbon dioxide and water
Signs of a chemical reaction include: color change, gas production (bubbles), temperature change, precipitate formation, or light emission
A synthesis reaction combines simpler substances into a more complex one: A + B -> AB
A decomposition reaction breaks a compound into simpler substances: AB -> A + B
A single replacement reaction: A + BC -> AC + B (one element replaces another in a compound)
A double replacement reaction: AB + CD -> AD + CB (ions from two compounds exchange partners)
The mole is a unit of measurement: 1 mole = 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number)
Reaction rate increases with higher temperature, higher concentration, greater surface area, or addition of a catalyst
Enzymes are biological catalysts (usually proteins) that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up
Oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons. They always occur together in redox reactions (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain)
Activation energy is the minimum energy required for a chemical reaction to begin; catalysts lower the activation energy
Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it will shift to partially counteract the change

common_errors.wrong: matter is created or destroyed in chemical reactions
common_errors.correct: The law of conservation of mass states that matter cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

common_errors.wrong: a catalyst is used up in the reaction
common_errors.correct: A catalyst speeds up a reaction but is not consumed. It is recovered unchanged after the reaction.

common_errors.wrong: dissolving sugar in water is a chemical reaction
common_errors.correct: Dissolving is a physical change. The sugar molecules remain intact; they are just dispersed among water molecules.

common_errors.wrong: rusting and burning are unrelated processes
common_errors.correct: Both rusting and burning are oxidation reactions. Rusting is slow oxidation of iron; burning is rapid oxidation.

common_errors.wrong: chemical reactions always happen instantly
common_errors.correct: Reactions occur at different rates. Some are nearly instantaneous (explosions), while others take years (rusting) or millions of years (fossil formation).

common_errors.wrong: a chemical equation is balanced if it has the same number of molecules on each side
common_errors.correct: A balanced equation has the same number of each type of ATOM on both sides, not necessarily the same number of molecules.

facts.statement: A solution is a homogeneous mixture where a solute (smaller amount) is dissolved in a solvent (larger amount)
Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves more substances than any other common liquid
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature
Solubility generally increases with temperature for solids in liquids, but decreases with temperature for gases in liquids
A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout (like saltwater); a heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts (like trail mix)
Concentration measures how much solute is dissolved in a given amount of solution; molarity (M) = moles of solute per liter of solution
A colloid is a mixture where particles are small enough to stay suspended but large enough to scatter light (e.g., milk, fog, gelatin)
A suspension has larger particles that will settle out over time if not stirred (e.g., muddy water, salad dressing)
Like dissolves like: polar solvents (water) dissolve polar and ionic solutes; nonpolar solvents (oil) dissolve nonpolar solutes
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods: filtration, evaporation, distillation, chromatography, or magnetism
An alloy is a solid solution of two or more metals; bronze (copper + tin) and steel (iron + carbon) are common alloys

common_errors.wrong: solutions are always liquids
common_errors.correct: Solutions can be any state of matter. Air is a gas solution. Steel is a solid solution. Soda water is a liquid solution with dissolved gas.

common_errors.wrong: all mixtures are solutions
common_errors.correct: A solution is only one type of mixture (homogeneous). Suspensions and colloids are mixtures that are not solutions.

common_errors.wrong: mixing always creates a chemical reaction
common_errors.correct: Mixing substances often creates a mixture (physical change), not a chemical reaction. Dissolving salt in water is mixing, not reacting.

common_errors.wrong: oil and water don't mix because water is heavy
common_errors.correct: Oil and water don't mix because water is polar and oil is nonpolar. Polar and nonpolar substances do not dissolve in each other.

facts.statement: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-containing compounds; carbon can form up to four covalent bonds, allowing an enormous variety of molecules
Hydrocarbons are molecules made of only carbon and hydrogen; methane (CH4) is the simplest hydrocarbon
Fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) are hydrocarbons formed from ancient organisms over millions of years
Polymers are large molecules made of repeating units called monomers; plastics, proteins, and DNA are all polymers
The four major types of biological macromolecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids
Carbohydrates (sugars and starches) are made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen; they are the body's primary energy source
Proteins are polymers of amino acids; there are 20 different amino acids that combine to make all human proteins
Lipids (fats and oils) are not soluble in water; they store energy, insulate the body, and make up cell membranes
Plastics are synthetic polymers; most are not biodegradable and persist in the environment for hundreds of years
Ethanol (C2H5OH) is the alcohol in alcoholic beverages; it is produced by yeast fermentation of sugars
Carbon can form long chains, branched structures, and rings, which is why there are millions of different organic compounds

common_errors.wrong: organic means the food has no chemicals
common_errors.correct: In chemistry, organic refers to carbon-containing compounds. All food contains chemicals. The term 'organic food' refers to farming practices, not chemistry.

common_errors.wrong: all carbon compounds are organic
common_errors.correct: Some carbon compounds (CO2, carbonates, cyanides, diamond, graphite) are traditionally classified as inorganic.

common_errors.wrong: plastics are natural materials
common_errors.correct: Most plastics are synthetic (man-made) polymers derived from petroleum. A few bioplastics are made from plant materials.

common_errors.wrong: fats are always bad for you
common_errors.correct: Fats (lipids) are essential for health. They store energy, protect organs, and form cell membranes. Unsaturated fats are generally healthier than saturated fats.

facts.statement: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space; it exists in different states and forms
A physical property can be observed without changing the substance (color, hardness, density, melting point); a chemical property describes how a substance reacts with other substances
A physical change alters appearance but not chemical composition (cutting, melting, dissolving); a chemical change creates new substances (burning, rusting, cooking an egg)
An element is a pure substance made of one type of atom; a compound is made of two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed ratios
Density = mass / volume; objects with density less than water (1 g/cm^3) float in water
The chemical formula for water is H2O, meaning each molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom
The chemical formula for table salt is NaCl (sodium chloride), made of sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio
The chemical formula for carbon dioxide is CO2, meaning each molecule has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms
A pure substance has a constant composition (elements and compounds); a mixture contains two or more substances not chemically bonded
Conservation of matter: in a closed system, matter is neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged; the total mass before and after a reaction stays the same
An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains the properties of that element; a molecule is two or more atoms bonded together
Intensive properties (density, boiling point, color) do not depend on the amount of substance; extensive properties (mass, volume) do depend on amount
The three subatomic particles are protons (positive charge, in nucleus), neutrons (no charge, in nucleus), and electrons (negative charge, orbiting nucleus)
An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means; there are 118 known elements
The law of definite proportions states that a compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass
Malleability means a material can be hammered into thin sheets; ductility means it can be drawn into wires. Metals typically have both properties
Flammability, reactivity with acid, and tendency to rust are examples of chemical properties because they describe how a substance changes into a different substance
Objects that have the same volume but different masses have different densities; a block of lead is denser than a block of wood of the same size

common_errors.wrong: dissolving salt in water is a chemical change
common_errors.correct: Dissolving is a physical change. The salt breaks into ions but the NaCl can be recovered by evaporating the water. No new substance is formed.

common_errors.wrong: a compound is the same as a mixture
common_errors.correct: A compound has elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (water is always H2O). A mixture has substances combined but not chemically bonded, in variable proportions.

common_errors.wrong: atoms can be seen with a regular microscope
common_errors.correct: Atoms are far too small to see with optical microscopes. They can only be imaged using electron microscopes or scanning tunneling microscopes.

common_errors.wrong: ice is a different substance from water
common_errors.correct: Ice, liquid water, and steam are all the same substance (H2O) in different states of matter. Changing state is a physical change, not a chemical one.

common_errors.wrong: all matter is made of the same atoms
common_errors.correct: There are 118 different types of atoms (elements), each with a different number of protons. Iron atoms are different from oxygen atoms.
